report.summary: Switzerland's Dec–Jan window gives the best light match within the Earth range; Peru matches light but has much higher sun. Mars lacks light data.

claims.text: The Shackleton rim receives very low sun, with half its sampled light below the horizon and the rest under 5 degrees.
Switzerland's 12-11 to 01-07 window gives the highest light_sim of the three Earth twins, inside the Earth range of 0.7389 to 0.9527.
Peru's 05-23 to 06-19 window also falls inside the range, but its median sun elevation is far higher than the target's, a weaker regime match.
The light model is analytic with no terrain shadowing, so the Mars twin's missing light_sim leaves Mars unassessed for light.

report.summary: Four field tests for the Shackleton rim: low-sun navigation at Switzerland, slope traverse at Peru, shadow ops at China, relay drill at Peru.

claims.text: Low-sun navigation drill at the Swiss highland, whose light match to the rim is strongest and whose window fits the target's sun-low conditions.
Slope traverse on the Peruvian Andes, the closest terrain match, with comparable local relief to the rim.
Shadowed-area operations drill at a Chinese highland analogue, using the rim site finder's low-sun pocket as the scenario.
Comms relay drill timed to the rim's low Earth elevation at landing, run from the Peru site using its nearest airport.

limitations: Sunlight uses an analytic model: circular orbit, no eccentricity, no local horizon or terrain shadowing.
Similarity is terrain shape only (slope, roughness, relief, curvature); not geology, chemistry or regolith.
Terrain is compared at one common ground scale; features smaller than the grid spacing are not seen.
Environment data (country, climate, airport) is a coarse proxy for logistics; no routing or permits checked.
Light model is analytic with no terrain shadowing.
Köppen climate classes are missing for all Earth candidates.
All Earth terrain similarities are modest.
Mars twin has no light or context data.
